Let $D$ be a nonempty finite regular oriented link diagram in an oriented $3$-sphere, with finite crossing set $C(D)$. Fix a unit viewing normal $n$ and orient the projection plane $P$ so $(u,v)$ is positive exactly when $(n,u,v)$ is positive in the ambient $3$-space. At a crossing $c$, define its sign as the sign of $\det_P(v_{\rm over},v_{\rm under})$, where the two nonzero projected tangent vectors follow the oriented over- and under-strands. Let $n_+$ and $n_-$ be the numbers of positive and negative crossings.

Set $\mathcal A=\mathbb Z[X]/(X^2)$, with $\deg(1)=1$ and $\deg(X)=-1$. Its unit, multiplication, counit, and comultiplication are
$$
\eta(1)=1,\qquad m(1\otimes1)=1,\quad m(1\otimes X)=m(X\otimes1)=X,\quad m(X\otimes X)=0,
$$
$$
\epsilon(1)=0,\quad\epsilon(X)=1,\qquad \Delta(1)=1\otimes X+X\otimes1,\quad\Delta(X)=X\otimes X.
$$
Thus $m$ and $\Delta$ have quantum degree $-1$, while $\eta$ and $\epsilon$ have degree $+1$.

Choose a total order $c_1<\cdots<c_n$ on $C(D)$. A resolution state is a function $v:C(D)\to\{0,1\}$; at $v(c)=0$ use the A-smoothing and at $v(c)=1$ use the B-smoothing from the Kauffman source chart. Write $|v|=\sum_c v(c)$, let $D_v$ be the crossingless resolution, and let $k(v)$ be its number of circles. Assign the state module $\mathcal A^{\otimes k(v)}$. For an edge $v\to v+e_j$ changing crossing $c_j$ from $0$ to $1$, use $m$ if the local smoothing merges two circles and $\Delta$ if it splits one circle, tensored with the identity on all other factors, and multiply this map by $(-1)^{\sum_{i<j}v(c_i)}$. The resulting direct sum has cohomological degree
$$i(v)=|v|-n_-$$
and the generator with circle labels $1$ or $X$ has quantum degree
$$j(v)=|v|+n_+-2n_-+\sum_{\text{circle labels }a}\deg(a).$$
This defines the normalized integral Khovanov cube and its candidate degree-zero cochain differential; the assertion that the differential squares to zero is a separate lemma.

The Frobenius identity that controls a merge-split face is represented by the two equal composites below. The diagram records the maps only; the proof verifies the equality on the basis $\{1,X\}^{\otimes2}$ and does not rely on the drawing.

```tikzcd
\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal A \arrow[r,"m"] \arrow[d,"\Delta\otimes\mathrm{id}"'] & \mathcal A \arrow[d,"\Delta"] \\
\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal A \arrow[r,"\mathrm{id}\otimes m"'] & \mathcal A\otimes\mathcal A
```

Let $D$ be a finite regular oriented link diagram, order its crossings as $c_1<\cdots<c_n$, and form the direct sum of state modules $\mathcal A^{\otimes k(v)}$ over all functions $v:C(D)\to\{0,1\}$. Here $\mathcal A=\mathbb Z[X]/(X^2)$, each crossing is changed from its A-smoothing at $0$ to its B-smoothing at $1$, and the edge map is the multiplication $m$ for a merge or comultiplication $\Delta$ for a split, multiplied by $(-1)^{\sum_{i<j}v(c_i)}$ on the edge at $c_j$. Then the sum $d$ of all edge maps satisfies $d^2=0$.

Let $(D,p)$ be a finite regular oriented diagram of a knot with a basepoint $p$ away from the crossings, and let $C(D)$ be its normalized integral Khovanov cochain complex. At each resolution state, let $X_p$ act by multiplication by $X$ on the tensor factor for the circle containing $p$, and by the identity on every other circle factor. The basepoint action is the direct sum of these statewise maps. Define the reduced cochain complex by
$$\widetilde C(D,p):=C(D)/\operatorname{im}(X_p),$$
with the same cohomological grading and with reduced quantum degree $\widetilde j=j-1$ for the class represented by a state whose basepoint circle is labelled $1$. Its cohomology is the reduced integral Khovanov cohomology $\widetilde{Kh}^{i,\widetilde j}(D,p)$. The unknot is normalized so that its reduced group lies in bidegree $(0,0)$.

Equivalently, cut the based knot at $p$ to a one-interval tangle. Put $M=\mathbb Z$ in quantum degree $0$ with $X\cdot1=0$. A resolution with $k$ closed circles and the distinguished interval is assigned $\mathcal A^{\otimes k}\otimes M$. An edge that merges a circle into the interval uses $m_M(1\otimes1)=1$ and $m_M(X\otimes1)=0$; an edge that splits the interval uses $\Delta_M(1)=X\otimes1$, where the circle factor is written first and the interval factor second. Edges not meeting the interval use $m$ or $\Delta$. This based tangle cube is the quotient complex above, with the stated quantum shift.

derivations.claim: **Meaning of every local map.** Use rectangles with top boundary points $1,\ldots,n$ and bottom boundary points $1',\ldots,n'$, both listed left to right. Let $I$ join $a$ to $a'$. Let $E_i$ join top $i$ to $i+1$, bottom $i'$ to $(i+1)'$, and all other $a$ to $a'$. In a product $UV$, $U$ is above $V$ and equal middle labels are joined. Thus $E_iE_i$ is $E_i$ with one disjoint middle circle, and $E_1E_2E_1$ is boundary-fixing planar isotopic to $E_1$; likewise with $1,2$ interchanged. For the latter assertion, trace top $1,2$ to one cap, bottom $1',2'$ to one cup, and top $3$ to bottom $3'$ along the remaining arc; there is no closed component. Contracting the intervening bends gives the stated isotopy. Close any of these matchings by a fixed exterior resolution. Order the resulting circle factors by the least arc label on each circle, using a fixed total order on all local and exterior arcs; factor permutations have no Koszul signs. A dot on an arc means multiplication by $X$ on the circle containing that arc. A saddle replacing an occurrence of $I$ by $E_i$, or conversely, means precisely $m$ on the two ordered circle factors if they merge, and $\Delta$ if they split, followed by the indicated factor permutation. All unmentioned factors have the identity map. This defines the maps below on every tensor basis $\{1,X\}^{\otimes k}$, even when several local arcs belong to the same global circle. In the based case use $M$ for the distinguished factor and [F2] for a saddle meeting it.

**Circle coordinates and neck cutting.** For a disjoint middle circle put its factor first and write $w=1\otimes w_1+X\otimes w_X$. If a saddle splits that circle from an arc carrying dot operator $x$, its map in these coordinates is $u\mapsto(xu,u)$; if it merges the circle into an arc carrying dot operator $y$, its map is $(w_1,w_X)\mapsto w_1+yw_X$. These follow from $\Delta(a)=1\otimes Xa+X\otimes a$ and $m(a\otimes b)=ab$. Two successive opposite saddles between the same two local arcs equal the sum of a dot on each arc. If the arcs are on distinct circles, this is the identity $\Delta m(a\otimes b)=Xa\otimes b+a\otimes Xb$: on $1\otimes1,1\otimes X,X\otimes1,X\otimes X$, both sides are $X\otimes1+1\otimes X,X\otimes X,X\otimes X,0$. If they are on one circle it is $m\Delta(a)=2Xa$. The same formulas with the distinguished factor reduced modulo $X$ prove the assertion in that case too. These are the exact tensor interpretations of the local neck-cutting identities, including when two dot positions are on the same circle.

**An explicit cancellation rule.** Suppose a differential between consecutive degrees has block matrix $\begin{pmatrix}\phi&\beta\\ \gamma&\delta\end{pmatrix}:A_0\oplus R\to B_0\oplus S$, with $\phi$ an isomorphism. Set $L(a,r)=(a+\phi^{-1}\beta r,r)$ and $T(b,s)=(b,s-\gamma\phi^{-1}b)$. These invertible integral changes of coordinates give $T d L^{-1}=\operatorname{diag}(\phi,\delta-\gamma\phi^{-1}\beta)$. Conjugate the adjacent differentials too. The equation $d^2=0$ and invertibility of $\phi$ imply that the incoming differential has zero $A_0$ coordinate and the outgoing differential vanishes on $B_0$. Thus there is a direct summand $A_0\xrightarrow{\phi}B_0$, contracted by $h|_{B_0}=\phi^{-1}$, $h=0$ elsewhere. Inclusion and projection of the remaining coordinates, conjugated by $L,T$, are chain maps $i,p$ with $pi=1$ and $1-ip=dh+hd$. This supplies actual chain maps and a homotopy for every cancellation used below, rather than merely an acyclicity assertion. If the blocks are homogeneous, these maps have quantum degree zero and $h$ has cohomological degree $-1$.

**RII: all four modules and signs.** Take two strands and order the crossing with states $(I,E)$ first, the opposite crossing with states $(E,I)$ second. The four states $00,01,10,11$ are $U=E$, $V=I$, $W=E$ with a middle circle, and $Z=E$, respectively. The local differential is $d^0(u)=(su,xu,u),\qquad d^1(v,w_1,w_X)=tv-w_1-yw_X,$ where $s:E\to I$ and $t:I\to E$ are the two saddles, $x$ is the dot on the arc from which the middle circle splits, and $y$ is the dot on the arc into which it merges. Here $C^1=V\oplus W_1\oplus W_X$; the minus signs on the $10\to11$ edge are exactly the cube sign for the second crossing. Step 2.1 gives $ts=x+y$, so these displayed differentials square to zero. Define $i(v)=(v,tv,0),\qquad p(v,w_1,w_X)=v-sw_X,$ with $i,p$ zero in other local degrees, and define $h^1(v,w_1,w_X)=w_X,\qquad h^2(z)=(0,-z,0).$ Then $d i=0$, $p d=0$, and $pi=1$. In degree zero $hd=1$, in degree two $dh=1$, and in degree one $dh+hd$ sends $(v,w_1,w_X)$ to $(sw_X,w_1-tv+(x+y)w_X,w_X)$, which is exactly $1-ip$. The surviving $V$ has local degree one and quantum grading increased by one; in the shift conventions of the question this is $[-1]\{-1\}$. Thus both acyclic pairs and the signed quotient are explicitly identified. The other crossing order follows by swapping the two cube coordinates with state sign $(-1)^{v_1v_2}$.

**RIII: ordered states and the first cancellation.** Let each crossing have states $(I,E_i)$, and form the word $121$ from top to bottom, with crossings ordered in that order. Write $P=E_1E_2$ and $Q=E_2E_1$. In degrees $0,1,2,3$ the ordered states are $I;\quad (E_1^{100},E_2^{010},E_1^{001});\quad(P^{110},(E_1\sqcup\bigcirc)^{101},Q^{011});\quad E_1^{111}.$ In the last term use the boundary-fixing isotopy $E_1E_2E_1\cong E_1$ of step 1.1. Denote a degree-one element by $(a,b,c)$ and the circle coordinates in state $101$ by $(w_1,w_X)$. Introduce four precisely located saddles: $u:E_1\to P$ inserts $E_2$ below $E_1$, $v:E_2\to P$ inserts $E_1$ above $E_2$, $w:E_1\to Q$ inserts $E_2$ above $E_1$, and $z:E_2\to Q$ inserts $E_1$ below $E_2$. Let $x$ and $y$ be the dot operators on the bottom cup and top cap of $E_1$, respectively. The degree-one differential is $d^1(a,b,c)=(-ua+vb,\ -xa+yc,\ -a+c,\ wc-zb),$ with output coordinates $(P,W_1,W_X,Q)$. Indeed the six cube edges are $100\to110$ with sign $-$, $010\to110$ with sign $+$, $100\to101$ with sign $-$, $001\to101$ with sign $+$, $010\to011$ with sign $-$, and $001\to011$ with sign $+$. The two edges to $101$ split the middle circle from the bottom cup or top cap, giving exactly the two displayed circle-coordinate pairs by step 2.1. The $101\to111$ edge has sign $-$ and merges that middle circle into the remaining through arc of $E_1E_2E_1$. Its $W_1\to E_1^{111}$ component is therefore $-1$, with its $W_X$ component minus the dot on that through arc. Cancel this $-1$ component by step 2.2. There are no remaining degree-three terms; the differential into $(P,W_X,Q)$ is the corresponding projection of the displayed $d^1$.

**The second cancellation and the common residual matrix.** In the resulting complex, the $c\to W_X$ component is $+1$. Cancel it by step 2.2: its row is $-a+c$, so the residual coordinate substitution is $c=a$. The retained degree-one coordinates are $(a,b)$, the retained degree-two coordinates are $(P,Q)$, and the differentials become $I\xrightarrow{\binom{s_1}{s_2}}E_1\oplus E_2\xrightarrow{\begin{pmatrix}-u&v\\ w&-z\end{pmatrix}}P\oplus Q,$ where $s_i:I\to E_i$ is the saddle inserting $E_i$. The first map is obtained from the original $d^0=(s_1,s_2,s_1)$ by deleting the canceled coordinate; it is compatible with $c=a$. Repeat both cancellations for $212$ with $1$ and $2$ interchanged. Its retained coordinates before reordering are $(E_2,E_1)$ and $(Q,P)$, with matrix $\begin{pmatrix}-z&w\\ v&-u\end{pmatrix}$. Swapping both pairs, without a sign, gives exactly the preceding matrix and the preceding $d^0$. The four entries refer to the same saddles on the same labelled boundary matchings: for instance $E_2\to P$ inserts $E_1$ above, and $E_1\to P$ inserts $E_2$ below, on both sides. Hence these are actual equal tensor maps by step 1.1, not identifications of unlabelled spaces. Their kernels, composites and signs need no further $\tau$ identities. Composing the two explicit cancellation maps and their inverses gives the RIII equivalence; the homotopy for a composite of retractions $(i_1,p_1,h_1)$ and $(i_2,p_2,h_2)$ is $h_1+i_1h_2p_1$.

**Quantum degrees.** A state of local height $r$ has quantum degree increased by $r$. In RII, $W_1$ has the underlying grading of $E$ increased by two, $W_X$ has the grading of $E$, and $Z$ has the grading of $E$ increased by two. Thus both canceled isomorphisms and the maps of step 3.1 preserve quantum degree. In RIII, $W_1^{101}$ and $E_1^{111}$ both have the grading of $E_1$ increased by three; $W_X^{101}$ and $E_1^{001}$ both have the grading of $E_1$ increased by one. The common residual complex has quantum increases $0,1,2$ in its three degrees. Every change of coordinates in step 2.2 is therefore homogeneous.

**Exterior differentials and the marked quotient.** Dots commute with every exterior saddle: $m(Xa,b)=Xm(a,b)=m(a,Xb)$ and $\Delta(Xa)=(X\otimes1)\Delta(a)=(1\otimes X)\Delta(a)$. Two saddles in disjoint local disks commute before cube signs, including when their participating arcs lie on a common global circle, by associativity, coassociativity and the Frobenius identity in [F1]. A middle circle being delooped is contained in the local disk, so no exterior saddle meets it. Boundary-fixing isotopies of the matchings preserve the labelled exterior arcs. All matrix changes, inverses of $\pm1$ blocks, projections, inclusions and contractions above therefore commute with unsigned exterior saddles and with $X$ at a fixed exterior marked point. The total differential, with local crossings first, is $d_{\rm loc}+(-1)^r d_{\rm ext}$ on local degree $r$. A local homotopy lowers $r$ by one, so its two exterior terms in $dh+hd$ cancel; local degree-zero maps commute with the signed total differential. These identities prove the same retractions for the total cube. The identities descend modulo $\operatorname{im}X_p$ because every map and every homotopy commutes with $X_p$; this argument does not assume that every local saddle acts trivially on the distinguished interval. It proves all assertions, integrally and choice-free.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

1. **Compact main case.** Let $M$ be a compact smooth manifold, possibly with boundary, let $N$ be a smooth manifold without boundary, let $F:M\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings that is constant near the ends of $I$, and let $W$ be an open neighbourhood of $F(M\times I)$ in $N$. Then there is an ambient isotopy $H:N\times I\to N$ with $H_0=\mathrm{id}_N$, every $H_t$ a diffeomorphism, $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ for all $t\in I$, $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ outside $W$ for every $t$, and $H_t$ stationary near the ends; if $F$ is constant near the ends with parameter $\varepsilon$, then $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ for $t\le\varepsilon/2$ and $H_t=H_1$ for $t\ge1-\varepsilon/2$.
2. **Relative form.** Let $N$ be boundaryless, $U\subseteq N$ open, $A\subseteq U$ compact, and let $F:U\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings whose track image is open in $N\times I$. Then there is a compactly supported ambient isotopy $H$ of $N$ with $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ on a neighbourhood of $A$ for every $t$.
3. **Boundary stratum.** If $N$ has boundary and $F(M\times I)\subseteq\partial N$, then the ambient isotopy of clause 1 can be chosen with every $H_t$ carrying $\partial N$ onto itself; if $F(M\times I)\subseteq N\setminus\partial N$, it can be chosen compactly supported in $N\setminus\partial N$.
4. **General isotopies.** For the same compact source (possibly with boundary) and boundaryless target as in clause 1, every smooth isotopy extends with support in a compact subset of any prescribed neighbourhood $W$ of $F(M\times I)$. The endpoint-constancy hypothesis and the stationary-end conclusion are both omitted; all other conclusions of clause 1 hold.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\mathcal F:M\times S\to N$ be a smooth family of maps and let $Z\subseteq N$
be an embedded submanifold. If $\mathcal F\pitchfork Z$, then the set of
parameters $s\in S$ for which the slice $\mathcal F_s:M\to N$ fails to be
transverse to $Z$ is a null subset of $S$.

Let $F:M^m\to N^n$ be smooth and let $Z\subseteq N$ be an embedded submanifold
of codimension $c$, and suppose $F\pitchfork Z$. If $c\le m$, then
$F^{-1}(Z)$ is an embedded submanifold of $M$ of codimension $c$ (possibly empty). If $c>m$,
then $F^{-1}(Z)=\varnothing$. In the first case, for each $p\in F^{-1}(Z)$,

$$ T_pF^{-1}(Z)=\{v\in T_pM:dF_p(v)\in T_{F(p)}Z\}. $$

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $F:C\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be a smooth
isotopy of a finite disjoint union of circles, constant near both ends, and
suppose both end projections under the fixed $\pi$ are regular. Arbitrarily
close to $F$ in the strong smooth topology there is such an isotopy $F'$, equal
to $F$ near the ends, whose projected slices have only these exceptional events:

(i) finitely many ordinary cusps, at distinct times; in a source coordinate
$x$, writing $g(x,t)=\pi F'(x,t)$, each satisfies
$g_x=0$, $\det(g_{xx},g_{xt})\ne0$ and
$\det(g_{xx},g_{xxx})\ne0$;

(ii) the **off-diagonal unordered** double-point locus is a smooth
one-dimensional manifold with boundary in the local-extension sense of
[[def-smooth-chart-atlas-and-structure-on-a-manifold-with-boundary]]; its boundary
consists exactly of the double points at $t=0,1$. Its interior is a manifold
without boundary, and its time projection has only finitely many
nondegenerate critical points, each an ordinary quadratic tangency of two
immersed branches;

(iii) finitely many transverse triple events, with all three pairs of
projected tangents independent, and no quadruple points.

No two exceptional events have the same time. All other slices are regular,
and between exceptional times their decorated diagrams vary by planar isotopy.

Let $F'$ satisfy the general-position conditions of
[[lem-a-smooth-isotopy-of-links-can-be-put-in-general-position]], with
exceptional times $t_1<\cdots<t_N$. Immediately before and after each event,
its regular diagrams differ, up to planar isotopy, by one oriented
Reidemeister move: R1 at an ordinary cusp, R2 at a quadratic double tangency,
and R3 at a transverse triple event. The regular intervals contribute planar
isotopies, and the moves preserve the over/under and orientation data of $F'$.
Consequently the end diagrams are connected by a finite sequence of these moves.

An **oriented Reidemeister move** is one of the following local replacements of
a regular oriented link diagram ([[def-regular-oriented-link-diagram]]),
performed inside a small closed disk while the diagram outside the disk is left
unchanged, and understood up to planar isotopy outside the disk
([[def-planar-isotopy-of-link-diagrams]]). All sign and orientation variants of
each local picture are included.

**(R1) Kink creation and deletion.** A single strand is replaced by a small
kink: two arcs crossing once and otherwise disjoint from the strand, with the
over/under datum of the new crossing as in the picture. The move is allowed in
both directions (create or delete the kink) and with both signs of the kink,
the sign being the sign of the crossing created. The orientations of the two
strands of the kink are the two possible consistent orientations through the
crossing, and all of them occur in the move list.

**(R2) Slide of two strands.** Two local arcs belonging to two strands are
replaced so that the number of crossings between those strands changes by two
of opposite signs: the standard picture slides one strand over or under the
other, creating or deleting the pair of crossings, with the two crossings being
the two possible signs in either order. All four orientation patterns of the
two strands at the two crossings are included.

**(R3) Sliding a strand past a crossing.** One strand is moved across an
existing crossing of two other strands, so that the crossing of the two other
strands passes from one side of the moving strand to the other; the three
crossings of the local picture keep their signs and the over/under data are
preserved. The three strands must have a consistent strict height order:
one is above both others, one below both, and the remaining strand is between
them. The cyclic over/under pattern is excluded. Every orientation pattern
and all six height orders of this standard local picture are included.

A local R2 or R3 picture is **braid-like** when, after a local coordinate
change and deformation, all participating strands run in the same positive
longitudinal direction. This is a local condition and does not require a
globally chosen braid axis. R1 is kept as a separate kink move.

The strands keep their orientations throughout every move. The union of the
three move types, together with planar isotopy, generates the equivalence
relation on diagrams used in the Reidemeister equivalence theorem below; the
moves are sometimes called R1, R2, R3 as above. Since every move changes the
diagram only inside a disk, it has a type and a finite list of local
orientation/sign variants, and each variant is realized by an ambient isotopy
as the next items show. The complete list of variants is required because the
Markov and Alexander constructions below act on oriented diagrams and count
signed crossings.

derivations.claim: **The endpoint realizations and the common cap.** Regard a planar diagram as a diagram on the projection sphere, and choose a small closed disk $U$ about its mark meeting the diagram in one crossing-free arc only. The complementary disk contains a proper interval diagram; its two endpoints can be put at any prescribed two boundary points by an orientation-preserving disk coordinate change, preserving the interval orientation. Realize its crossings at small distinct positive or negative heights in a thickening of that disk, and straighten short end collars. Round the thickening to a standard three-ball $B$. Closing the interval by a fixed unknotted arc in the complementary ball $B_*$ gives exactly the original diagram on the sphere: the two projected disks glue along their boundary and the cap is the single deleted arc. This operation changes no crossing, sign, or resolution; it replaces the marked circle in every resolution by one interval. Make these choices for both diagrams with the same $B,B_*$, endpoints and cap $J$. The cap and slightly longer knot collars may be chosen identical as parametrized embeddings at both ends. Indeed an orientation-preserving change of circle parametrization can prescribe its parametrization on an interval; it extends over the remaining interval by a strictly increasing smooth map. Such circle reparametrizations are isotopic to the identity, as seen by interpolating their increasing lifts $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, $f(x+1)=f(x)+1$, with the identity lift. Thus there is a smooth isotopy $F_t$ of the closed parametrized knots with these endpoint embeddings and this common source interval $J$. Reparametrize time to make it stationary near $0,1$. Here the existence of $F_t$ is exactly the hypothesis that the two closed diagrams represent the same oriented knot.

**Trivialize a moving ball, including its endpoint charts.** Along the track of the slightly enlarged source interval $J$, choose a smooth pair of normal vectors to the nonzero knot tangent, equal to the same standard pair near $t=0,1$. Such a pair exists on the rectangle $J\times I$: start with local transverse frames, extend them along the interval and then in time, and correct their terminal angle by a smooth rotation, equal to zero initially and to that angle terminally. The terminal angle has a smooth real lift on an interval. Regarding $S^3$ as the unit sphere in $\mathbb R^4$, use the explicit tube $(F_t(s)+u n_1(s,t)+v n_2(s,t))/\sqrt{1+u^2+v^2}$, with the two normals tangent to $S^3$. Its derivative is injective along the zero section. For uniformly small transverse coordinates it is an embedded tube; compactness gives a common width and excludes intersections with the rest of the knot outside the enlarged interval. Rounded end caps give a smooth family of embedded three-balls $b_t:B_*\to S^3$ about the cap, intersecting the knot in the chosen cap and its standard end collars. At the two stationary ends this family is the same specified ball chart: $b_0=b_1$. Apply [F1] to $b_t$ and, if necessary, a slightly larger ball chart, to get $H_t$ with $H_t b_0=b_t$. Then $G_t=H_t^{-1}F_t$ fixes the cap and its collar throughout. Its restriction to the complementary source interval is a proper-arc isotopy in the fixed $B=S^3\setminus\operatorname{Int}B_*$. At $t=0$ it is the first tangle; at $t=1$ it is $h$ applied to the second, where $h=H_1^{-1}|_B$ is a diffeomorphism equal to the identity on a boundary collar, because $b_1=b_0$ on the slightly larger ball. No identification of the terminal ball chart with an arbitrary initial chart has been assumed.

**Correct the terminal diffeomorphism on the arc.** Identify $B$ with the unit ball and choose the coordinate origin off the second compact arc $T$. The chart can have this property by a small interior change fixing its boundary collar. Since $h$ is the identity near the boundary, for $0<r\le1$ the maps $h_r(x)=\begin{cases}r h(x/r),&|x|\le r,\\ x,&|x|\ge r\end{cases}$ are smooth diffeomorphisms, agreeing smoothly at $|x|=r$, and equal to the identity on a fixed boundary collar. Put $h_0=1$. For $r$ less than the positive distance from the origin to $T$, $h_r|_T$ is exactly the identity. Thus $(s,r)\mapsto h_r(T(s))$ is a smooth isotopy of proper arcs even at $r=0$, although the ambient Alexander formula need not be smooth at $(x,r)=(0,0)$. Each slice is embedded, its endpoints and collars are fixed, and its final slice is $h(T)$. Reverse this arc isotopy and concatenate it with step 2.1, using stationary time changes at the join. The resulting smooth arc isotopy runs from the first tangle to the second relative to the same boundary endpoints and collars. This argument uses no claim that the diffeomorphism group of a three-ball is smoothly contractible.

**Projection and relative perturbations.** Choose the standard ball model as a rounded thickening of the projection disk, with the two fixed endpoint collars radial in that disk and with constant height. The rest of the compact arc track is in the interior of the ball. Shorten the protected collars if needed. Compactness then separates their projected endpoint neighbourhoods from every other branch: off a slightly larger source collar the radial coordinate in the disk is uniformly bounded away from its boundary. On the remaining transition collars the projection is still a fixed regular embedded arc. Reparametrize the isotopy in time to be stationary near its two regular end diagrams. In the finite-dimensional family of [F2], replace the time cutoff $\lambda(t)$ by $\lambda(t)\rho(s)$, where $\rho$ vanishes on the protected source collars and is positive on their complement. The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $D$ and $D'$ be regular oriented link diagrams.
Then $D$ and $D'$ represent equivalent oriented links if and only if $D'$ can be
obtained from $D$ by a finite sequence of planar isotopies and oriented
Reidemeister moves R1, R2, R3.

Let $D,D'$ be finite regular oriented link diagrams related by a planar isotopy or one oriented Reidemeister move. Let $\bar C(D)$ be the integral signed state cube before the writhe shifts, with cohomological degree $|v|$ and quantum degree $|v|+\sum\deg(a)$, and normalize it by $C(D)=\bar C(D)[n_-]\{2n_--n_+\}$ to obtain the state degrees $i=|v|-n_-$ and $j=|v|+n_+-2n_-+\sum\deg(a)$. Before normalization, a positive type-I curl gives $\bar C(D_+)\simeq\bar C(D)\{1\}$, a negative type-I curl gives $\bar C(D_-)\simeq\bar C(D)[-1]\{-2\}$, a type-II move gives $\bar C(D_{II})\simeq\bar C(D)[-1]\{-1\}$, and a type-III move gives an unshifted equivalence. Consequently the normalized complexes are bigraded chain homotopy equivalent. If $D,D'$ are based knot diagrams and the move disk is disjoint from the basepoint, the same chain homotopy equivalence descends to their reduced quotient complexes, equivalently to the cut-tangle complexes with interval module $M=\mathbb Z$, $X\cdot1=0$.

For a finite regular oriented link diagram $D$ with $n$ ordered crossings, the procedure that enumerates all $2^n$ smoothing states, assigns one copy of $\mathcal A=\mathbb Z[X]/(X^2)$ per resolution circle, places a generator in degrees $i=|v|-n_-$ and $j=|v|+n_+-2n_-+\sum\deg(a)$, and sums the signed merge or split edge maps terminates after finitely many operations. Its output is a finite direct sum of finite-rank free abelian groups with a differential of bidegree $(1,0)$ satisfying $d^2=0$; hence it is a bounded bigraded cochain complex.

A chain map $f:C_\bullet\to D_\bullet$ is a **chain homotopy equivalence** if
there exists a chain map $g:D_\bullet\to C_\bullet$ such that
$$g\circ f\simeq1_C,\qquad f\circ g\simeq1_D.$$

Such a map $g$ is called a **homotopy inverse** of $f$.

Let $D,D'$ be finite regular oriented link diagrams related by a planar isotopy or one oriented Reidemeister move. Let $C_\bullet,D_\bullet$ be chain complexes in an abelian category
$\mathcal A$, and let $f,g:C_\bullet\to D_\bullet$ be chain maps. A **chain homotopy**
$s:f\simeq g$ is a graded morphism of degree $1$,
$$s_n:C_n\to D_{n+1},$$

$$f_n-g_n=d^D_{n+1}s_n+s_{n-1}d^C_n.$$

[[def-hom-complex-of-chain-complexes]].

there exists a chain map $g:D_\bullet\to C_\bullet$ such that
$$g\circ f\simeq1_C,\qquad f\circ g\simeq1_D.$$

Such a map $g$ is called a **homotopy inverse** of $f$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Let $D$ be a finite regular oriented diagram of a link with $n_+$ positive crossings, $n_-$ negative crossings, writhe $w=n_+-n_-$, and $n=n_++n_-$. For each resolution state $v$, let $k(v)$ be its number of circles and let $D_v$ use the A-smoothing at coordinates $0$ and B-smoothing at coordinates $1$. Put $\delta=-A^2-A^{-2}$ and define the normalized bracket
$$f_D(A):=(-A^3)^{-w}\sum_{v:C(D)\to\{0,1\}} A^{n-2|v|}\delta^{k(v)-1}.$$
For integral unreduced Khovanov cohomology, define $\chi_q(Kh(D))=\sum_{i,j}(-1)^i\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb Z}Kh^{i,j}(D)q^j$. For reduced cohomology use its basepoint quantum grading $\widetilde j$ and define $\widetilde\chi_q=\sum_{i,\widetilde j}(-1)^i\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb Z}\widetilde{Kh}^{i,\widetilde j}(D,p)q^{\widetilde j}$. Under $q=-A^{-2}$ and $t=q^2=A^{-4}$,
$$\chi_q(Kh(D))=(q+q^{-1})f_D(A),\qquad \widetilde\chi_q(D,p)=f_D(A).$$
Thus the unreduced unknot factor is $q+q^{-1}$ and the reduced unknot factor is $1$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $A$ and $t$ be formal variables and $K$ a
nonempty oriented link. At each crossing of a regular diagram $D$ use the
source chart with over-strand southwest-to-northeast: A joins top and bottom
endpoints with coefficient $A$, and B joins left and right endpoints with
coefficient $A^{-1}$. A state $S:C(D)\to\{A,B\}$ assigns one smoothing at every
crossing; let $a(S)$ and $b(S)$ count these choices and $|S|$ count the
resulting circles. Fix a unit viewing normal $n$ and orient the projection
plane $P$ so $(u,v)$ is positive exactly when $(n,u,v)$ is positive in the
ambient oriented $3$-sphere. Define
$$\operatorname{sgn}(c)=\operatorname{sgn}\det_P(v_{\rm over},v_{\rm under}),
\qquad \operatorname{wr}(D)=\sum_c\operatorname{sgn}(c),$$
$$f_K(A)=(-A^3)^{-\operatorname{wr}(D)}
  \sum_{S:C(D)\to\{A,B\}}A^{a(S)-b(S)}(-A^2-A^{-2})^{|S|-1}.$$
For an $n$-strand braid $\beta$ whose oriented closure is $K$, let
$e:B_n\to\mathbb Z$ be the homomorphism $e(\sigma_i)=1$, where $\sigma_i$
is the positive geometric Artin half twist. Let $H(n)$ be the type-A Hecke
algebra with generators $T_i$, quadratic relation $T_i^2=(v-1)T_i+v$, braid
relations, and distant commutation, and let $\pi_n(\sigma_i)=T_i$. Its
normalized Markov trace $\operatorname{tr}_n$ satisfies
$\operatorname{tr}_n(1)=1$, cyclicity, tower restriction, and
$\operatorname{tr}_{n+1}(xT_n)=z\operatorname{tr}_n(x)$. Define the library
Jones value by
$$V_K(t)=s^{e(\beta)}\left(-\frac{s^2+1}{s}\right)^{n-1}
\operatorname{tr}_n(\pi_n(\beta))\Big|_{v=s^2,\,z=-1/(s^2+1),\,t=s^2},$$
where $s=t^{1/2}$. With $A=t^{-1/4}$, these values satisfy
$$V_K(t)=f_K(t^{-1/4}).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For every nonempty oriented link $L$, the bigraded integral groups $Kh^{i,j}(L):=H^i(C^{*,j}(D))$, where $D$ is any finite regular oriented diagram of $L$ and $C(D)$ is the normalized Khovanov cochain complex, are independent of the choice of $D$ up to bigraded isomorphism.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $K$ be an oriented knot and let $(D,p)$ and $(D',p')$ be finite regular oriented diagrams of $K$ with basepoints away from all crossings. Then the reduced integral groups $\widetilde{Kh}^{i,\widetilde j}(D,p)$ and $\widetilde{Kh}^{i,\widetilde j}(D',p')$ are isomorphic for every $(i,\widetilde j)$. In particular, they are invariant under Reidemeister moves supported away from the basepoint and under transport of the basepoint along the knot.

derivations.claim: By [A1] and [F1], full AC supplies AC$_\omega$. Hence [F4] identifies the bigraded groups computed from any finite diagram $D$ with $Kh^{i,j}(L)$, and in the knot case identifies the reduced groups with $\widetilde{Kh}^{i,\widetilde j}(K,p)$ for every allowed basepoint. The fixed-diagram complexes have finite rank and bounded support, so their rank Euler sums are finite.

By [F2], those Euler sums are $(q+q^{-1})f_D(A)$ and $f_D(A)$, respectively. By [F3], $f_D(A)=V_L(A^{-4})$ under the stated full-AC hypothesis. Substituting $q=-A^{-2}$ and $t=q^2=A^{-4}$ gives exactly the two formulas in the Statement. For a crossingless unknot the unreduced complex has its two generators in quantum degrees $1,-1$, whereas the reduced interval module has one generator in reduced degree zero, so the respective factors are $q+q^{-1}$ and $1$. Since [F4] makes the groups diagram- and basepoint-independent, these are the claimed link and knot Euler characteristics.
